claims.text: Tungsten-based alloys are intended for use in fusion plasma-facing components.
Increasing helium implantation density decreases high-temperature plastic strain.
Increasing helium implantation density decreases high-temperature fracture toughness.
Implanted helium forms nanoscale bubbles at defects and within the tungsten-alloy matrix.
Helium bubbles impede dislocation motion and climb at elevated temperature.
Helium bubbles promote microcrack formation.
Impeded dislocation motion and climb limit ductile flow and reduce toughness.
Specimens will be fully recrystallized, have low initial impurity content, and have controlled grain size.
Varying helium doses introduced by ion implantation, with an unimplanted control, will isolate helium exposure.
Mechanical testing will be performed at 800–1200 K in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
In-situ electron microscopy will track dislocation activity and crack nucleation.
Increasing helium levels will decrease uniform plastic strain by on the order of tens of percent relative to helium-free controls.
Increasing helium levels will lower fracture toughness relative to helium-free controls.
Reductions in plastic strain and toughness will correlate with helium-induced nanobubble density.
The proposed mechanism should dominate in single-phase tungsten-based alloys at moderate helium retention levels achievable by ion implantation under near-surface fusion conditions.
At sufficiently high helium concentrations, large-scale crack coalescence may complicate the proposed dose-response relationship.
The quantitative dependence of plastic strain and toughness on helium concentration remains underdetermined.
Interactions between helium implantation and neutron-induced damage are uncertain.
The comparison will use helium doses of 0, 1×10^21, and 5×10^21 He atoms/m² and measure elongation, fracture toughness, and bubble size and density.
The hypothesis is falsified if implantation produces no statistically significant change in plastic strain or toughness, or if bubble formation does not correlate with dislocation-based deformation.
